Well, ancient flier that I am, I guess it's time (and place) for my kite story. Few people know about this; for one thing, not many would be interested.

So when I was about 12, during a beautiful summer in British Columbia, there was a period of about a week with warm, strong winds. Unusual. We had lots of gusty bits, but I spent 'way too much time running around and around the field next door trying to get something into the air. But this week, was golden, it was fantastic. One day I tied my kite to a fence post and went in for lunch and came back and it was still up there, happy as a clam.

Anyway, on the day of which I speak, I had a beautiful box kite, about three feet high and a foot square, red and yellow and blue paper and balsa, and my dad had found a strong nylon line that had to be close to 1000 feet long. And the wind, wonderful wind. Oh, boy, I got out there and the box kite took to the air like it was made to be weightless, beautiful. Got out almost to the end of the line, the kite had surpassed the edges of the farmer's field and it was flying over foreign country, the forest on the other side of the powerhouse road, beyond the reservoir. I remember thinking about how long it was going to take me to wind it in again...and wondering how hard it would be to pull....

I had an hour or so, or it felt like it, with the kite majestically pasted on the blue sky, steady wind, not very, you know, performance oriented, but that's fine; I was having a twelve-year-old zen experience. Mindlessly staring at the line curving out of sight, and the kite mysteriously happy with itself 'way over there...wherever there was. When in a moment, the line went slack, just broke somewhere out there, and the kite...well, it just launched. It didn't come down, it just flew away at about the same elevation until it disappeared over the forest as the curvature of the earth took it. And part of me with it.

It was such a magnificent loss, I couldn't be sad, because it was perfect. Locked in time, a part of me will always be there, watching as the kite achieves a life of its own....
My kite story, from 1960 or so

TIL A Layer 7 DDoS attack mimicks real human behavior making it harder to detect and mitigate
I read somewhere else that these attacks are done using bots. Can someone explain how bots are able to do the really complicated captchas like "select all the pictures of pizza"?

The bots aren't solving captchas. They just load up the front page, and various posts, etc. The problem is that they do it much more frequently than legitimate users.

In a nutshell, each page load costs the server (in this case, voat) a small amount of resource usage (bandwidth, CPU, disk, RAM, etc). Layer 7 DDoS attacks load up pages to use up those resources, to deny those resources to legitimate requests. They do so using bots (computers infected with the botnet owner's virus). This way the requests look legitimate because they come from computers that belong to normal users.

"Layer 7" refers to the user interface layer, so the difference between a DDoS attack and a "Layer 7 DDoS attack" is that the Layer 7 DDoS attack targets the "Application" layer. That is it runs an actual browser, renders the page, etc. It then takes that page render and throws it away instead of displaying it to the user. A layer 7 attack costs the attacker a lot more resources than a lower layer attack because rendering the page is a lot more computationally expensive than just requesting the page and throwing away the results (which would be layer 4 or 5) or just sending a flood of bogus data to the target's IP (layer 3).

In summary, each bot in a botnet has a specific amount of bandwidth, CPU, disk, RAM, etc. The attacker tell the bot to use those resources to use up the target's resources. What Cloudflare does is that in order to render the page, the attacker has to solve a math problem. Solving this math problem uses up a small but significant amount of CPU. Since the botnet has a limited (but large) amount of resources, it runs out of resources more quickly this way, and can request fewer actual pages, reducing the number of page requests that hit the target's servers.
